maintopic: SALES FROM SOUTH AFRICA AT PREMIUM OF $6.50 PER FINE OUNCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SALES FROM SOUTH AFRICA AT PREMIUM OF $6.50 PER FINE OUNCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) asked whether in view of the approval by the international monetary fund of the sale by South Africa of newly-mined alloy gold to be used only for industrial or professional work at a premium of $6.50 a fine ounce over the fund's price of $35 a pure ounce, the government would extend the same right to Canadian gold producers. At that time I told him I had seen the press report but had no official information on the matter. I said I would make an inquiry. I have done so, and I find that the international monetary fund has not in fact approved any specific sale of gold at a premium by South Africa. Yesterday the international monetary fund issued a statement in that regard which, for the purpose of the record, I shall place on Hansard. That statement is as follows:
Following certain press reports about a gold sale at premium prices made by South Africa, the international monetary fund wishes to make it clear that it has not approved any specific gold sale at a premium price.
The fund was consulted four months ago by the South African government with regard to a proposed plan to sell semi-processed gold at premium prices for industrial, professional, or artistic purposes. The fund advised the South African government that it was "disturbed by the fear that the trade in semi-processed gold which is contemplated by the South African government would involve considerable sales of gold at premium prices for other than legitimate industrial, professional or artistic purposes. It felt that this would almost certainly be the consequence if the proposed transactions are to be on a scale sufficient to ensure an appreciable profit to . . . gold producers.
In these circumstances," the fund added, "the fund believes that South Africa should not engage in the proposed plan unless it is satisfied that it can take effective measures to ensure that gold sold under the plan will in fact be used for bona fide and customary industrial, professional or artistic purposes."
The South African government informed the fund over this past week end that it has agreed to sell a quantity of semi-processed gold at a premium price. However, in the light of the information submitted by South Africa, including the prices and quantities involved, the fund has found it necessary to get in touch with South Africa with a view particularly to determining whether the safeguards adopted are, in the fund's opinion, adequate to ensure that any gold sold will in fact be used for bona fide and customary industrial, professional and artistic purposes.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRODUCTION PROGRAM FOR 1949

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRODUCTION PROGRAM FOR 1949
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture, of which I have already given notice. Is it the intention of the government to give a lead to western farmers as to what grains should be grown for 1949? If so, will the minister make a statement to the house in that regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRODUCTION PROGRAM FOR 1949
speechtext:
As the hon. member has said, a copy of his question was sent to me this morning. The practice of the provincial and federal governments in the years preceding the war was that the provinces had the most to do with production. They gave more direction in that regard than did the federal department of agriculture. At the beginning of the war however it was thought advisable that considerable direction should be given by the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa. Therefore we held conferences annually, beginning in 1939, with the provincial authorities, farming organizations, the farm press and representatives of the federal Department of Agriculture, upon which occasions we discussed all questions relating to the necessity for greater production of one product as compared with another during the period of the war. That practice continued until two years ago, when we decided to hold conferences during the first week of December of each year and discuss the probable or possible program in connection with agricultural production for the succeeding year.
A conference was held on December 6, 7 and 8 last, at which the provinces and the farm organizations were fully represented. The agricultural press was represented, and for part of the time the daily press also. The question of the production of different farm products was fully discussed, and at the end of the meeting it was unanimously agreed that the direction that should go out from all sources should be to the effect that the acreage that had been utilized in the

Inquiries of the Ministry previous year lor the purposes of producing different crops, or in connection with livestock, would be suitable for the coming year.
But there was one possible change. Where western farmers had seeded a considerable acreage in flaxseed in the years during the war and up to last year, it was considered, in view of our experience, that it might be well for them not to seed so much flax; and to the extent that they desisted from seeding flax it might be wise to put their acreage into coarse grains which would be required in greater and greater volume in the years ahead.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TERMS OF UNION WITH CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPROVAL OF TERMS OF UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 11, to approve the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TERMS OF UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not delay for more than a few moments the passage of this important and historic bill. I am fairly familiar with that magnificent island which is to be our tenth province; yet I feel that I should speak very briefly. Newfoundland was represented at the Quebec conference of 1864, when the four provinces of Canada, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-decided to enter confederation. I often recall the words of Sir Ambrose Shea, who was one of the two Newfoundland representatives. So far as they were concerned they were satisfied with the proposals and would have joined the confederation, but did not have the authority to do so at that time. Ever since 1864, well-wishers of confederation, both in Newfoundland and in Canada, have looked forward to this day. I am sure we are all happy indeed at the prospect that lies before us. I will not repeat the exact words of Sir Ambrose Shea, but he said that, looking into the future, he could hardly describe the great vista that opened before him, in the realization of what confederation would mean to his province and to Canada.
Confederation has turned out to be something much greater than anything Sir Ambrose Shea could have visualized. At that time British Columbia was not a part of Canada, nor were the three western provinces. If Sir Ambrose could have foreseen the Canada of today, of which Newfoundland will be the tenth province, he would have seen that we have one river, the Mackenzie, with the largest basin, all in the same country, on the whole continent of North America. Some will say at once that I am forgetting the Mississippi, but the basin of the Mississippi is not all in the United States; part of it is in Alberta and part of it is in Saskatchewan. The Mackenzie river is wholly in Canada.
Canada also borders the largest lake in the world, although not all of it is in Canada. Eleven thousand square miles of the 31.000

Newfoundland
square miles of Lake Superior are in Canada. We also have exceptionally high mountains. At the time of Sir Ambrose Shea, the St. Elias group of mountains between Yukon and Alaska, which rises to a great height, were not known to be in Canada. The highest mountain in that range is Mount Logan, with a height of 19,850 feet. Canada has inexhaustible resources. What would Sir Ambrose Shea have seen? He would have seen that the Canada of today is one of the largest national areas in the world. I believe we are exceeded only by Russia, including Siberia, but we are larger than European Russia. Together with Newfoundland's 152,000 square miles, we shall now have approximately 3,750,000 square miles. Including Newfoundland and Labrador, the population of Canada will be very close to thirteen and a half million people.
We have grown to be a very great state both in area and in population. Our cousins to the south have a larger population, but continental United States is more than 750,000 square miles smaller than Canada. Including Alaska it is perhaps 150,000 square miles less. I do not know whether it is there now because the building may have been blown down in the late war, but I often think of the inscription on the money exchange building in London near the famous monument to the great fire. The inscription is: "The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof." When God made this part of the world he must have been thinking of the fulness of this country, because, interpreting fulness as material wealth, in many respects we surpass the whole world. For instance, there is nickel; in Canada we have approximately nine-tenths of all the nickel in the world.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TERMS OF UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext: Asbestos.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TERMS OF UNION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Asbestos is to be found in the eastern townships of Quebec; we have approximately eighty to ninety per cent of all the asbestos in the world. Our country is rich in all minerals. It is only a few years ago that Canada produced over $200 million worth of gold, and at the same time the production of all minerals in Canada exceeded $500 million.
In coming into confederation, therefore, Newfoundland is joining one of the great countries of the world, and with the new province we shall make a greater country still. To me it is a solemn occasion when I think that from 1864 to 1949, a period of over eighty years, many efforts have been made to make confederation complete. When this bill passes the house, as it will, confederation will be complete. As the years roll on, those who come after us will refer to that great year when the confederation of Canada was completed as the fathers of confederation visualized it in 1864 and 1867. We in this

house will be off the scene at that time, but we will be remembered for our humble parts in bringing to pass what the fathers of confederation sought to accomplish.
A short time ago I came across a few lines which seem to suit what is running through my mind at the moment. I will quote them:
For the structure that we raise Time is with materials filled.
Our todays and yesterdays Are the blocks with which we build.
The blocks with which this structure has been built are the men who carried on the negotiations for union from 1864 onward, the fathers of confederation of those days, representing Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, and those who carried on the present negotiations. Down the years all these men were labouring to build this fine structure which has finally come to pass. Now we and our brothers in Newfoundland may look forward to the certainty of rising to even greater heights.
Today we add another 1,500 miles to our Atlantic front. A moment ago when the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was giving the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) some admonitions with respect to his trip to Washington, I thought of something else the Prime Minister might take up when he is in the United States. I hesitate to mention it, and I do not suppose he would have time to do it anyway, but on some future occasion he might consider negotiating with the United States in an endeavour to bring in the panhandle which cuts five hundred miles off our western coast. That is something for the future. If it should ever come to pass, what a majestic country we would have from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
As a humble Canadian, Mr. Speaker, I am proud and happy that the vision which these great men have had all down the years, and which our present leaders have worked so hard to fulfil, at last has become a reality.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Agricultural Products Act to extend the operation of the act for a period of one year.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
I take it the minister will want to introduce this resolution with a somewhat comprehensive statement, and I suggest that the appropriate time to do so would be before Mr. Speaker leaves the chair, having

in mind that this procedure has been generally followed so far this session.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
The bill it is intended to introduce if the resolution is adopted is short and simple, providing that the provisions of the act concerning the sale and export of agricultural products shall be extended to cover an additional year. The provision made last session was to the effect that this bill was to cover the period to March 31, 1949. The new bill will provide that the period be extended to March 31, 1950.
The reason a bill of this kind is required is the fact that the activities with which it deals were carried on during the war under the War Measures Act. When the War Measures Act came to an end provision was made for some of the matters that had been dealt with under that legislation to be continued under the special measures act. A special measures act was introduced to deal with many of the matters that had been carried on by order in council under the War Measures Act, but so far as the sale of agricultural products by contract was concerned, a special act dealt with those, and it is a bill to extend that act with which we are dealing at the moment.
At this stage it might be advisable to point out that the bill itself defines the agricultural products which are covered by it, by saying:
"Agricultural product" means any product of agriculture, except wheat, and includes "feeding stuff" within the meaning of The Feeding Stuffs Act of 1937.
I quote that in order to point out that the wheat contract does not come under this bill. That contract has been dealt with under the wheat board act. In addition I think I should point out that section 3 of the bill provides:
Subject to any regulations that may be made by the governor in council, the minister may
(a)	sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof pursuant to any agreement made by the government of Canada with the government of such country or with such agency and for these purposes may purchase agricultural products and make such arrangements for the purchase, sale or export of agricultural products as he considers necessary or desirable;
(b)	on behalf of the government of any country or any agency thereof purchase or negotiate contracts for the purchase of agricultural products;
(c)	by order require any person to give such information respecting his facilities for the storing or processing of agricultural products and at such times as the minister may designate in such order;
(d)	enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products.

Each is still carrying out a contract with respect to one important item; therefore it is necessary to continue in existence the three boards we had during the war period, and it is necessary to deal with matters having to do with bacon, eggs and cheese in any discussions we may have concerning what is to be done in the year 1949-50.

As the minister has said, this resolution to amend the Agricultural Products Act to extend the operation of the act for a period of one year is really a continuation of the War Measures Act for certain purposes.
Part of the preamble of that act, brought in in 1947, says:
-the government of Canada entered into agreements for the sale or export of food supplies to other gov-

Agricultural Products Act emments or agencies thereof, which agreements still continue in force; and whereas certain orders and regulations were made by the governor in council under the authority of the War Measures Act and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, for the purpose of enabling Canada to carry out the said agreements; and whereas the said orders and regulations will expire on the 31st day of March, 1947, and it is necessary by reason of the existing national emergency that parliament confer authority-
In another paragraph the act points out that,
"agricultural product" means any product of agriculture, except wheat, and includes "feeding stuff."
Another clause of the act reads:
-the minister may sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country-
The entire authority is vested in the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) under the act as passed in 1947.
As a companion to this act, there is an act known as the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, which was merely a transitional measure to provide for the maintenance of price levels and by which a revolving fund of $200 million was established. This amounts to less than 10 per cent of the amount this government has prevented the agricultural producers of Canada from receiving by means of controls, embargoes and government marketing programs. In other words, since 1942, this government has caused the farmers to lose over $2,000 million, which cannot be easily recovered. This figure is over three times the total expenditure of the three prairie provincial governments during those same years. It is a sizeable sum of money which the farmers have contributed by marketing their goods through government agencies.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture told the members of the house that, by taking less than the prevailing world price for bacon, wheat and dairy products, et cetera, the Canadian farmer would be assured of good overseas markets after the war. Mr. Speaker, today Britain is purchasing great quantities of bacon from Poland and Denmark, beef from the Argentine and wheat from Russia. The Canadian overseas market for apples, fruits and potatoes has been entirely lost. Beef on the hoof and certain other agricultural products in Canada have decreased in price during the past five months by over 20 per cent, yet the cost of living index has reached an all-time high and now stands at 159-6. I do not think the consumers can accuse the agricultural producer of responsibility for that situation.
With respect to the cost of living today, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speak-

ing on December 11, 1947, as reported at page 215 of Hansard, said:
. . . we have continued our control on wheat by making a contract with Great Britain. . . . the price of feed grains to farmers in eastern Canada and in other parts of Canada has borne about the same relationship to wheat as the government would have been compelled to place upon oats and barley if they had followed the suggestion of the organized farmers . . .
On the same page, he said:
. . . the most effective control on feed grains is the fact that there is an established value for wheat.
The Minister of Agriculture, speaking on this Agricultural Products Act on December 19, 1947, said this at page 503 of Hansard:
There has always been the closest check made on the relationship between wheat and feed grains, and between feed grains and products fed from feed grains, when all these contracts were being negotiated.
At page 504 he said:
We have the No. 2 price, which is the price under which wheat is sold to countries outside Great Britain. The No. 2 price is one we are able to charge because of certain conditions, the first of which is that we have sold an average of 150 million bushels a year to Great Britain over a period of four years . . . That is the first factor which makes it possible for us to ask a price, rather than to go on the market and sell at a price which is offered.
The second reason is that we are able to say it has a higher intrinsic value;
I quote now from page 505 of Hansard:

During 1946, the percentage of the total imports of Great Britain supplied by Canada for the various commodities is as follows: wheat flour 57 per cent; bacon, 38 per cent; carcass meat, which is chiefly beef, 7-6 per cent; eggs in the shell, 15 per cent; dried eggs, 15 per cent; cheese, 24-2 per cent and evaporated milk 10-5 per cent. It is recognized throughout this country that the government, year after year, neglected the United States market. They systematically refused to sell to those who wanted our foods and, at the same time, created a heavy deficit of United States dollars.
In 1946, during the discussions on the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement, this party stood alone in opposition to forcing the Canadian wheat producer to carry the entire financial burden. There were no ifs, so far as we were concerned. We predicted exactly what would happen, despite the protestations of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and of our socialist friends, the C.C.F.
If the terms of the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement had been carried out according to the adjustment clause, the price for the fourth year of the agreement would have been over $5 per bushel. However, it has now been arranged to ignore the terms of the contract and leave the final settlement until after the next Canadian general election. According to press reports Canada to date has received $640 million for offshore purchases under ECA. During the past twelve months, most of this money has come from Washington. Fifty per cent of the total of $322 million has been used to buy wheat, for the most part on British order.
I think that is proof of the serious situation facing the producers of this country. I should now like to refer to the price of international farm implements. In the letter I read reference was made to that. In 1945, just prior to the wheat agreement, these implements were selling for the following


prices: the three plow tractor sold for $1,630.60; the combine for $3,150; the twelve foot swather for $394.60; the harrow plow for $401.75. In 1948, after the agreement the same three plow tractor sold for $2,179.75; the combine for $4,219.85; the twelve foot swather for $519 and the harrow plow for $488.
Of course today prices have gone considerably higher. I have comparisons as to the number of bushels of wheat the United States farmer has to produce to buy these same implements as compared with the Canadian farmer. To purchase in Canada a Farmall M tractor, international company tractor, required 1,225 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 710 bushels of wheat. To purchase a 3-furrow international tractor plow in Canada required 151 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 82 bushels. To purchase a 24-run international double disc seeder in Canada, required 270 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 146 bushels. To purchase a 10-foot international binder in Canada required 333 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 184 bushels. To purchase the same tractor in Canada would require slightly over the price of eleven finished 1,000-pound steers, while in the United States the same type of tractor would require the proceeds of only slightly over six such animals. It would require 46 select hogs weighing 210 pounds in Canada or 26 such hogs in the United States to purchase the same type of tractor. With respect to federal taxes, direct and indirect taxes amounted per capita to $22.41 in 1913, and in 1939 the per capita had risen to $38.67. added to the cost of production and the cost of living in Canada, a fact which government officials have ignored in compiling the cost of living index and of production for this nation.
I should like to say to the government backbenchers who are now making vehement speeches asking for the reduction of taxation that they had an opportunity a year ago to vote against the tax measures of this government. They apparently think, along with their government, that they can bleed the people of this nation for four years and then play Santa Claus in the fifth year just prior to an election.
A year ago we proposed a motion giving hon. members an opportunity to vote against that if they had wished.
The Canadian federation of agriculture, in their brief of December 14, 1948, showed that the urban consumers have made great gains over the past fifty years in their food purchasing power per hour of work. Hourly wage rates last September could buy 60 per cent more food than in 1913 or 68 per cent more than in 1920. The farmer does not begrudge the gains of urban groups, provided these gains are not made at the food producers' expense, and provided these gains are in line with increases in productivity.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Many people in this country have said that the Minister of Agriculture, who has objected to my referring to wheat, made the greatest gamble ever made by any individual or government in the history of the world when he sold this country short some 600 million bushels of wheat, of which 440 million bushels had not even been seeded and for
Agricultural Products Act which no man or woman had any idea what the future price would be. On the basis of that contract he has attempted to tie in the value of all other agricultural products, coarse grains, beef, pork, dairy products and poultry products; they have all been tied in with the price of wheat. Anyone can read the remarks he made, as reported in Hansard on December 19. The tying of the value of those agricultural products to the artificial price of wheat which had been created by this government has cost the agricultural producers of this country considerably over $2,000 million, an amount which they have no way of recouping. Statistics will prove that. I am one of those who believe that the government should reimburse those producers who have made altogether too great a contribution, along with paying their own share of the taxes for the subsidization of consumers during the war years.
A few minutes ago the Minister of Justice had something to say and I should like to call him as a witness on my behalf. I have before me the report of a speech which he made on March 31, 1948, not quite a year ago, when he was discussing the wheat board act. I intended to quote it but as that seems objectionable to some of my hon. friends across the way I shall just state that he pointed out that the wheat board was created in the interests of the wheat producers of this country and was so used until 1943, when by order in council this government decided to use it for some other purpose. Ever since then they have been using it to keep down prices.

Page four of this published speech, which was pretty well distributed throughout the province of Manitoba, reads:
The Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 set up the wheat board as the voluntary agency of the wheat producers, charged with the fiduciary responsibility to secure for farmers who shipped wheat to it the best price available consistent with the promotion of the sale and use of Canadian wheat in world markets; and until the change made by order in council in 1943 all the business of the board was conducted on this basis.
During the war, on September 28, 1943, by order in council P.C. 7942 your government provided that the wheat board was to become a compulsory agency or monopoly where it had formerly been a

Agricultural Products Act voluntary agency; and that it was to become the agent of the Crown, instead of continuing as it had been the agent of the wheat producers. Later in 1947, the provisions of this order in council were incorporated into the provisions of the wheat board act where they now appear as section 4, ss. (2), reading as follows:
"4. (2) The board is for all purposes an agent of His Majesty in the right of Canada and its powers under this act may be exercised by it only as an agency of His Majesty in the said right."
And again:
The effect of these provisions in practice was that the wheat board was changed from being an agency of the wheat producers charged with responsibility for getting the best possible price, to an agency of the government, getting a price which would be fixed by the government, that is a political price, using that phrase in its best sense. Since 1943, when the wheat board was changed from being an agency of the wheat growers to being an agency of the government, the price paid to Canadian farmers for their wheat has been determined as a matter of government policy in the light of such consideration as the food agreements with Great Britain and the advantages of holding down the cost of living in Canada, and doubtless other equally worthwhile reasons.
Then I quote from page 13 as follows:
The holding down of the Canadian cost of living and the embargo upon the exports of farm products to the United States are examples of policies which are intelligible and perhaps wise. But they are also national policies, the cost of carrying out which should be paid, in our opinion, by the whole body of the Canadian people and not by the Canadian farmers only.
I hope he is able to bring that about now as a minister of the government. Farther down on the same page appears the following:
What other products of Canada, either primary or secondary, is the government going to fix the price of and leave the burden of carrying the difference between the government price and the market price upon the producers of those products? If this is a good policy for wheat and pork and beef and poultry products, and now oats and barley, why is it not a good policy for copper, newsprint, fish, tractors and farm implements?
It will be seen that the minister and I do not differ on everything all the time. I am pleased to call him as a witness and I hope he can exercise enough authority with his colleagues to see that these producers are reimbursed for the altogether unfair contribution they have made for so many years to the consumers of Great Britain and Canada. I am sure that is only a fair and reasonable request.
I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks that this was a continuation of the war emergency measures. It will give power to the Minister of Agriculture to arrange, through the cabinet, all these contracts and to do what he pleases with what our farmers produce in order to fill them. When the act was brought into being he told us that the representatives of many farm organizations were then in Ottawa asking for marketing
[Mr. Ross (Souris) .1

legislation. That was not the type of legislation they were asking for, or, if they were, they have changed their minds.
Last year the farm federation of Canada presented to the government a brief asking for a natural products marketing act. As my time is just about up I shall not attempt to read the brief, although it is important. The Bennett government brought such an act into being but when the Liberal government took over they sent it to the courts where it was declared to be ultra vires.
The farmers of the country want enabling legislation so that they may have control of the marketing of their own products. They are asking for legislation similar to that passed in 1934 by the Bennett government, which legislation was then known as the Natural Products Marketing Act. The resolution follows:
Whereas the organized farmers of Canada, through the provincial and Canadian federations of agriculture, have on many occasions since the court decision that the 1934 marketing act was ultra vires, requested the dominion government to enact comprehensive marketing legislation that would enable farmers to market their products in an orderly manner;'
And whereas the government has not seen fit to pass such legislation and has not as yet given any logical reason why this request of the farmers should not be granted;
And whereas eight of the nine provinces of Canada have shown by their actions in passing provincial legislation that, in their opinion, such legislation is necessary and in the public interest;
Therefore be it resolved:
1.	That the Canadian federation of agriculture again puts on record its belief that dominion marketing legislation, to supplement the provincial acts, is urgently necessary if the farmers of Canada are to be placed in a position equal to that of other elements in the community.
2.	That once more the Canadian federation of agriculture requests the dominion government to introduce at the next session of parliament comprehensive marketing legislation that will make it possible for groups of farmers to control the marketing of their own products rather than be at the mercy of speculative interests.
3.	That failing assurances that such legislation will be introduced, the Canadian federation of agriculture demands to know the reasons why the government of Canada, by its lack of action in this important matter, is apparently of the opinion that the farmers of Canada should be kept permanently in an inferior position as compared with other elements of society, and that such reasons be published for the information of all Canadian farmers.
I think that is sufficient proof, Mr. Speaker, that farmers in general across Canada are not satisfied with this act. I know personally that they are very much dissatisfied with the state of confusion that has been created by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government under this act. They are very fearful about their future. Their costs of production have risen consistently. I have given some instances with respect to the cost

or farm implements. The cost of farm labour is higher today than at any time in history, although I am sure we want to see all workers well paid in this country. Then there is the cost of fuel oil, the twine they use, and everything else which enters into agricultural production. These things have not been taken into account at all at this time.
The bureau of statistics issues figures showing the income of the agricultural population, but that is gross income. In many cases it would be very significant to have the net income and compare it with the gross. I say the farmers of the country are very fearful about their future. They are not satisfied with what has been done in the past under this act, and under the orders in council of the government. They are entitled to a great deal better act at this time. Therefore I disapprove of this measure as it is drawn, and I think there should be other marketing legislation provided in the interests of producers.

Agricultural Products Act the Canadian people know, of the wonderful part the British people played in saving democracy, and that they at the time practically stood alone. Certain misgivings arise in the minds of many people, now that peace has been declared, when they see Britain sending metals and war planes to soviet Russia, and leaving the markets of Canada alone, or out of their purchases. They do not want any British Columbia canned fish, lumber or eggs. While the Minister of Agriculture has been criticized, I feel that inwardly hon. members will agree with me that he put up the best fight that anyone could with the British authorities.
The British are great traders, as we all know. I do not have to remind you of that, and they usually send people from the north of Scotland to do the trading. When they get around a conference table they drive a pretty hard bargain. While the contract with Great Britain is not all that it should be, and we in British Columbia are certainly displeased with the British egg contract, I think it is to the minister's credit that he brought back to this country as good a contract as he did. It is not my duty, however, to warn the British people or to warn our people, but I would not like to see the lack of trade agreements bring about differences between the people of Canada and the people of Great Britain. I think that while we owe a great debt of gratitude to the British people, the British nation also owes some recognition to the Canadian people for what Canada did during the war.
Owing to the fact that the people of Great Britain and Europe required food, we were naturally encouraged by the government, at the request of Great Britain, to increase our agricultural production. In British Columbia, because of sentiment, shall we say, because also of our desire to help the British people, and at the request of the government, we increased our poultry flocks. Throughout the Fraser valley, and all through the province, men went into the poultry business who had not been in it before. But now it appears the British are not prepared to buy as many of our eggs, nor our lumber or canned salmon.
I think we can take a great deal of credit for one thing, Mr. Speaker. Of all the eggs that reach the British market, none can compare in quality with our Canadian eggs. So much is that the case that I understand this year two great egg-exporting countries, Eire and Denmark, are sending experts to Canada to ascertain how this country produces such fine eggs. So it is hard to understand why the British people or the British government would not want more of this excellent product.


I rose particularly to make a suggestion, and I ask the Minister of Agriculture to give it very serious consideration. Under this act, in order that the contracts for the various agricultural products may be fulfilled, we have been debarred from a free market. In British Columbia, at least at the present time, we could sell our eggs and poultry at much higher prices in the United States than the special products board will pay or even than Canadians are willing to pay for these products. If no better contract with Great Britain can be obtained, we are asking that we in British Columbia should be allowed to find that higher market, and that we should not be barred from that lucrative business across the boundary line. In all sincerity I ask the minister to give the people of British Columbia at least that consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the measure before the house merely extends for another year the operation of the Agricultural Products Act, though the discussion has covered a somewhat wider field. I want to state, first of all, that as far as we here are concerned we feel that this act is a poor substitute for a natural products marketing act on a national scale, but in view of the fact that it is necessary in order to carry out the contracts that have been or may be entered into, we are prepared to support the extension of this act.
I believe the real issue is whether or not this government or this parliament is going to take steps to provide a marketing act on a nation-wide basis, so that all commodities may be sold in such a way that the producers will receive the fullest possible benefit from their production. I agree with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), in that it is the responsibility of the government to reimburse or compensate the farmers who have incurred losses in the past few years owing mainly to the fact that the government has failed to carry out its price stabilization policy. But I cannot agree with the argument, which is at least implied, that the farmers would like to see the open market return. The fact is that the Canadian federation of agriculture has asked this parliament, or at least the individual members, to pass a marketing act; and if I understood the hon. member correctly he indicated that he was in favour of a natural products marketing act. If we are in favour of an act to provide for the orderly marketing of farm products we cannot argue at the same time that we are for the open market, because we cannot be on both sides of the fence at once. I am sure it is within the memory of all hon. members that when the Canadian Wheat Board Act came up-which was an endorsa-tion in an indirect way of the British wheat

agreement-hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party to my right voted for it. One hon. gentleman here says he did not; there may have been one or two.

I am not speaking of the wheat board; I am speaking of the wheat board act, which implied approval of the British wheat agreement, because it was only under the wheat board act that we could carry out that agreement at all. There is no use trying to wiggle out of that position; this house did support the wheat board act and at the same time, tacitly if not expressly, endorsed the British wheat agreement. But the basis on which that was done, as far as western agriculture was concerned, was that we were entering into an agreement with Britain for the purpose of having a guaranteed market at a guaranteed price over a period of time, and that in return we were willing to accept a price lower than the world market price at that time. We wanted stability; and it was the responsibility of the government to see that such stability was maintained.
That is where the difference of opinion arises today. As far as I am concerned it is not a question of whether we should be for or against orderly marketing. I am for it. It is a question of whether the government has carried out its end of the bargain. I contend that it has not, and to that extent I agree with the hon. member for Souris. But I do not agree with him if he implies that the Canadian farmers wish to get back to the open or speculative market; I cannot go along with him on that.
Since the statement has been made that no one to my right supported the British wheat agreement, let me quote what was said by the then leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken) on August 14, 1946:
I rise at this time to criticize the government's wheat policy. But before doing so, let me say this, with respect to the United Kingdom wheat agreement. Any agreement such as this which tends to level out the inequalities, and the wide fluctuation of prices in the past, is a step in the right direction.
Agricultural Products Act
That pretty well makes this house unanimous in approving the principle behind the British wheat agreement, if not the details themselves. The then leader of the official opposition agreed that any contract which would tend to cut out fluctuations or inequalities in marketing was a step in the right direction, and I agree with him one hundred per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that as I proceed I shall have no difficulty in keeping within the terms of your ruling. The chief point at issue so far as we are concerned, as I mentioned at the outset, is whether the proposed bill to follow this resolution will go far enough to provide the type of marketing legislation the farmers of Canada desire. We contend it does not go far enough. We contend it is necessary to have a natural products marketing act on a nation-wide basis, with marketing boards in the various provinces. These boards would have producer representation on them and would be a means of carrying on a nationwide system of interprovincial and export, trade.
In 1945, the Canadian federation of agriculture presented a draft bill to all members' of:: the house, a copy of which I have in my hand. This draft bill sets out in a general way the type of legislation the farmers are requesting.. According to the_ wording of this draft bin, it would have as its purpose the improvement of the methods and practices of the marketing of natural products in interprovincial trade within Canada, and in export trade, to make provision for the regulation and control of the trade and commerce therein, and to make further provision in connection therewith. Then, the draft bill sets out the way in which the act would operate.
Recently, the president of the Canadian federation of agriculture made this statement.

Agricultural Products Act as reported in the Plural Co-operator of Ontario:
Are we again to see food products-real wealth- backing up, clogging markets and bringing distress to farm families while populations elsewhere suffer undernourishment or stark hunger simply because they have the wrong currency, and because the rules of the financial world won't let one currency be freely converted into another?
We thought we had learned the lesson in two world wars that what is humanly and physically possible should also be financially possible.
The challenge to this parliament is to make it financially possible to carry out what has been made physically possible. The production is here. Under the old system of marketing, the farmers have often produced themselves right out of the market. In other words, they have produced so much that the cry of overproduction has gone up.

speechtext: That is what happened to two crown companies in Saskatchewan; they had to close down.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with this argument. Let us continue with this argument, instead of deploying in all directions.
Sir John Boyd Orr has proven his argument that there has never been enough food in this world to satisfy all the hungry people. There has always been starvation, famine and lack of proper nourishment in the nations of the world. Our health department shows that, in this country, which is supposed to be the bread basket of the world, there was before the war a highly disturbing proportion of undernourishment amongst our own population. That being so, no one can say the larmers produce too much. It is simply due to the fact that agricultural production has not been efficiently distributed to the markets of the world. It is also due to speculations in the market when the motive was to make a profit out of food production rather than to deliver food to the people who needed it.
The president of the Canadian federation of agriculture has challenged this parliament to get around the dollar difficulty. He does not say how that can be done, but it is not his function to do that. He is placing the problem before us.
On the 19th of March, 1948, a very interesting exchange took place between the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and the then minister of reconstruction who is presently the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I should say that a question was asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), and this is recorded on page 2418 of Hansard:
I want to ask the minister one simple question.
I am much impressed, as X hear him talk, as to the position of the milling and other industries. He
[Mr. Zaplitny. 1

says that the government will do this and the government will do that, and that as long as these people will do what they are told, they will be well off. Perhaps they will. Would I be wrong in calling this a highly socialistic measure?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
State marketing is socialism, yes, if
you like. But it is hard to be different in a world that at the moment is following state marketing for reasons which I think are largely beyond their control. There are currency problems, credit problems and a number of factors, which are driving countries to state marketing at the present time.
Now, that happened last March. Events since then have proven, to a very great extent at least, that what the minister said at that time was quite correct. Regardless of the type of trade we may like to have, we are governed to a certain extent by the type of trade that is prevalent or in vogue in the rest of the world. If Great Britain and the other countries have dollar difficulties and cannot buy from us in dollar currency, it is up to us to find a way in which we can dispose of our marketable products without involving dollar difficulties.
One of the ways in which this might be accomplished was suggested by my leader in a recent speech in which he pointed out that we could make bulk trade agreements with Britain and other countries on the basis of blocked sterling which would not involve immediate payment. By whatever manner it is done, I think it is highly important that this parliament realize the importance of this problem so far as the agriculture of this country is concerned. We shall be faced again with this artificial surplus, food piling up while people are going hungry. It is going to be the old story of hunger amidst plenty.
There are those who argue we should get around it by going back to the open market system. These people may have some reasons for presenting that argument, but recent events seem to argue strongly against it. This morning I clipped an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, headed:
U.S. administration seeks to stabilize slump in farm prices.
The dateline is Washington, February 9: The Truman administration moved today to shore up farm prices ordering an investigation of the commodity market slump which it attributed in part to "speculative influences."
Would the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) or any other member of this house suggest that we follow the United States pattern of open market trading when it is breaking down right before our eyes and the government of the United States has to step in to save the producers? In western Canada we pride ourselves that, at least, the farmers many years ago foresaw this condition. The

mere mention of the Winnipeg grain exchange to a farmer is a challenge to come out and roll up your sleeves, because they will not any longer fall for that open market story so assiduously proposed by certain interests which are spending millions of dollars to publicize the glories of the open market and to attack the wheat pools and the co-operatives of western Canada. I do not think they will fall for that propaganda. I would be very sorry if any hon. member coming from western Canada, and representing a rural constituency on the prairies, would lend himself to be the vehicle for the arguments of the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Let me quote some figures to supplement those quoted by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). He quoted figures to show how many bushels of wheat were required to buy certain farm implements in the United States as compared with Canada. Let me remind him that from 1931 to 1935 we did not have the Canadian wheat board. We had the wide open free enterprise speculative system of selling grain. Here are some of the figures that it is well worth while to keep in mind. In 1931 it took 715 bushels of wheat to buy an 8-foot binder.

I have not the figures for the same years in the United States, but we are now dealing with Canada. We must face the question in a reasonable way. It is not an ideological matter; it is a matter of being practical. The farmers have realized that they cannot trust the speculative market to handle their produce because it is not being handled for the purpose of giving farmers the greatest return for their labour nor to give the consumer the cheapest food possible. It is being handled for the purpose of extracting the greatest possible profit out of the labour of the farmer and out of the consumer of food.
Having come to that conclusion, the next logical step is to find another system by which their food products may be marketed. Various members have proposed various schemes, but in order that there may be no doubt about where we stand on the question I wish to place on record the six points
Agricultural Products Act adopted by our national convention last summer when it dealt with agricultural markets. They read as follows:
The C.C.F. therefore proposes:
1.	A system of guaranteed or forward prices. Minimum prices will be established well ahead of the planting or breeding season to enable farmers to plan their production in advance without worrying about market fluctuations.
2.	Enactment of a national marketing act, and the establishment, with producer and consumer representation, of marketing boards for all agricultural products, which enter into interprovincial or export trade.
3.	Orderly world marketing based on long-term international agreements.
4.	Assistance in the development of co-ops, commodity groups and other farm organizations for orderly marketing.
5.	Elimination of speculation in the marketing of 'foods.
Adoption of the "ever normal granary" principle. The federal government will assume the major responsibility for financing the storage of sufficient feed and seed grains to ensure a continuous supply. It will also construct strategic storage facilities itself and will assist provincial and local governments as well as farmers to build supplementary facilities in all appropriate areas.
If these proposals were adopted-and I think this parliament could adopt them without doing any violence to its political views -they would be practical steps which would help the farmer to dispose of his products to the very best advantage to himself and to the ultimate consumer.
I wish to emphasize that the time has come when scientific methods can be introduced for the processing and the storage of foods which could not be stored some years ago. We have advanced in the field of refrigeration, cold storage and processing to the point where it is possible to carry a far larger proportion of our surplus than was possible some years ago, and we should take full advantage of that. Surely in a world such as we live in, when no one knows when the next famine will come, or where, when no one knows when peace may be violated, it would be only sensible and humane to provide large storage facilities for surplus foods; which could be used in times when production fails. That, together with machinery set up on a nation-wide basis for the proper and orderly marketing of farm products, is what the farmers of Canada want.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on the resolution, but as several other hon. members have spoken I should like to say a few words. The general position of this group was placed before the house by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) and I am not going to take up time by repeating what he said. There are one or two aspects of the demand for national marketing legislation which particularly concern some of my constituents.
First of all I must say that I agree with much of what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) had to say with reference to the position in which the poultry producers find themselves at this time. The same situation which he said was developing in the riding of New Westminster is develop-

ing in the riding of Kootenay West. Many people are going out of poultry production because under the terms of the special products board's contract they cannot produce eggs at a profit, especially during the last year with the increased price of grains.
That is a serious situation to a great number of these people who have invested several years of hard work and in some cases considerable money in building up poultry farms. I do not believe there is any other section of agriculture that is in such an unstable position. I sympathize with the poultry producers because I am under the impression that, owing to the smallness of their number and organization as compared with the grain growers and beef producers and so on, their voice is not listened to in Ottawa to quite the same extent. Before proceeding to say a word or two with regard to the fruit industry I wanted to point out to the minister the serious situation that is facing many of the poultry producers in British Columbia.
For five or ten minutes I am going to speak, not only as a member of this house but as a pioneer settler in the district from which I come, as one who has been connected with the fruit industry for over forty years and who has seen it develop-I am speaking of the apple industry now-from one that was able to ship only a few hundred boxes to one that had a total production of over 8 million boxes in 1947.
The demand for marketing legislation is not a demand by a few members of parliament who represent various parties. The hon. members who have spoken represent the points of view of the agricultural producers in their ridings. They are simply representing the urge and the wish, based on past experience, of the farm producers in their districts.
Experiments have been carried on in British Columbia for many years in developing marketing machinery and various forms of selling organizations. We fully expected that as soon as the war was over a natural products marketing act would come into being. There is a sense of disappointment throughout the fruit-growing industry that that has not happened, particularly at this session. The growers, and rightly so, were very expectant in that regard.
I should like to review the situation briefly, and in doing so I speak of the fruit industry because that is the industry of which I have the greater knowledge. What the growers are asking for is based on experience and knowledge. What they are asking the government to do is to pass legislation which will give them an opportunity to carry their efforts

into a wider field. They will do the work and they will see that the act functions.
The pioneers in my district started to plant orchards about 1905. There were a few trees planted before that, but I think it is safe to say that the commercial planting of orchards in the interior of British, Columbia commenced about 1905. By 1916 we were producing about 1,000,000 boxes. In 1947 we produced approximately 8,000,000 boxes of apples. By that year peaches were up to about 150,000 packages; prunes, 1,000,000 packages and pears over 600,000 packages. That was a short period of time in which to see an industry build up to that extent from zero.
I can remember the early days quite well. For several years we found excellent markets in the local lumbering and mining camps and in the small villages throughout the district. In about five or six years, possibly by 1911 or 1912, considerable shipments were made to the prairies. For a few years we found sufficient outlet for our surplus apples on the prairie markets, apples going east as far as Winnipeg.
By 1913 or 1914 it became obvious to the fruit growers of the interior of British Columbia and to the officials of various organizations representing them that some form of orderly marketing was necessary. As a result of that realization the first large organization in British Columbia was formed known as the Okanagan United Growers. While that was its name its membership included the whole Kootenay group. That organization functioned for a few years, but not very satisfactorily owing to somewhat inexperienced management and the increasing need for marketing legislation.
In 1923 a larger organization was formed. A prominent United States citizen of that date, whose name I think was Aaron Shapiro, came to Kelowna to lecture us on the benefits of a large united co-operative movement. At that time I thought it was simply a waste of time and money, but he had the evangelistic spirit and as a result the Associated Growers of British Columbia was formed. That organization functioned for a few years fairly satisfactorily, but it was realized that voluntary co-operation alone was not sufficient to satisfactorily market the fruit and vegetables produced in the area.
By 1926 there was a growing demand for provincial marketing legislation. Organization meetings were held throughout British Columbia and growers expressed themselves as being definitely in favour of provincial marketing legislation. In 1927 the first provincial marketing act in Canada was passed in British Columbia. That act operated to a limited extent for about two years when it was declared to be ultra vires.
Agricultural Products Act
Then we come to 1934, when the federal government passed the dominion Natural Products Marketing Act. After two years, I understand, that act was declared to be ultra vires. In 1935 a new British Columbia act was drafted and passed and found to be sound law by the privy council. Since that date we have had no difficulty so far as the British Columbia legislation is concerned.
Out of that act developed the tree fruits board of British Columbia, and out of that board has been established Tree Fruits Limited of British Columbia. The authority upon which Tree Fruits Limited is based is twofold. First it receives authority for its organization from the tree fruits board, and secondly by virtue of the three-way contracts signed between growers, shippers, and Tree Fruits Limited. At the present time Tree Fruits Limited is the sole marketing agency in British Columbia for the sale of tree fruits. All this time it was realized that we would have to go further afield to achieve success.
In the matter of provincial legislation and co-operative organizations great success has been achieved. There is no question that the history of marketing in the interior of British Columbia is a credit to any group of growers, and a credit to the executives and officers who have guided and controlled the organizations throughout the years. Every problem has been approached in a constructive way. At this time I want to stress particularly that in British Columbia we have been most fortunate in having a particularly efficient, capable, and fine type of officials administering the fruit organizations.
Then the growing demand for a dominion marketing act arose. In 1938 the Canadian federation of agriculture asked the federal government for the first time to give effect to a dominion marketing act, and it has been asking for that legislation ever since. I believe when the first proposals were made by the Canadian federation of agriculture there was not unanimity throughout all Canada as far as agricultural producers were concerned, but owing to the experience of recent years, the realization of the benefits that accrued under the War Measures Act, and other wartime legislation, and the possibilities of development in somewhat different form for peacetime purposes, there has now been recruited, in support of dominion marketing legislation, the greater body of the farmers in this country.

Whereas the need for dominion marketing legislation is now more urgent than ever before as farmers face changing conditions with increasing production costs and declining demand for many of their products, and
Whereas at a public meeting held at Kelowna, B.C., on May 17, 1948, the dominion Minister of Agriculture stated that the government was prepared to enact marketing legislation that would meet the demands of Canadian farmers;
Therefore be it resolved that this 1948 convention of the B.C. federation of agriculture instructs the Canadian federation of agriculture to register an emphatic protest with the Canadian government against the unreasonable delay in introducing marketing legislation, which legislation is now recognized by all main political parties as being necessary and desirable.
That, if unable to obtain from the government a definite promise that a satisfactory marketing act will be introduced at the earliest possible opportunity, the federation insist upon being given valid reasons for the ignoring of the wishes of the farmers of Canada by failure on the part of the government to furnish them with a legal basis upon which the marketing of their products could be stabilized.
That resolution was carried unanimously. Since that meeting I have had the opportunity, with the member for Yale (Mr. Jones), to attend the meeting of the Canadian horticultural society and I am sure he will endorse all I am saying here today. At that meeting we heard the disappointment expressed by the delegates attending it representing fruit interests from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I am not quite sure of the terms of their resolution, but they adopted one expressing


their disappointment with regard to the failure of the government to pass a marketing act, and urging that all parties be asked to declare their stand on the matter before the expected federal election.
I think this demand has been a matter of slow evolution. It is not legislation that is being asked for as a result of hasty and unconsidered action. It is the culmination of a long period of evolution, experience and practice in the marketing of agricultural products in this country, co-operative experience, experience with provincial marketing legislation, experience with war measures, experience with commodity agreements, and so on. As I have said before, I believe the people have laid the foundation for such legislation as a result of their own efforts, their own work, and their own experience. I urge the minister and the government to give consideration to their plea, and by so doing forge the necessary link between provincial and international marketing.

Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate at the present time because I am anxious to place before the house the position of a great number of people who live in my constituency, and who are engaged in a particular form of agricultural pursuit, namely, that of the poultry industry. I do not think that it is exaggerating to say that there is no branch of agriculture which is facing greater uncertainties and greater difficulties at the present time than the poultry industry. It is because of the condition which has been produced that I wonder whether the result of the activities carried out under the Agricultural Products Act justifies the continuation of that act for another period of time. It was only a few years ago that representatives of the government toured Vancouver island urging various people to go into the poultry business, and urging poultrymen to increase their production. During the war the poultrymen co-operated in every possible way, and in the years succeeding the war every effort was made by them to increase production, and to produce eggs and other poultry products at a time when those products were most urgently required in the United Kingdom market, as suggested by representatives of the Department of Agriculture who traveled about the province.
As a result, egg production was increased from something like one million dozen before the war to as much as eighty-nine million dozen during the war. An endeavour was made also' to meet the desire of the department that early chicks be produced. This could be done on Vancouver island, because of our climate, but to do so it was necessary to expand plant, to construct different types of poultry houses, and so on, all of which

meant an increased outlay by the poultrymen. They constructed new buildings, invested in new types of equipment for breeding and hatching purposes, and also invested in new and better types of stock. After the war many veterans entered this business, investing their savings and gratuities.
About that time the cost of all materials began to rise; and even though it cannot be laid right at the door of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), this government must take some responsibility for those increasing costs; the cost of living, the cost of construction materials, equipment and labour required for the additional buildings and to look after the increased flocks. Very shortly after that the price of feed began to increase. When the subsidies on feed grain were removed the price jumped $10 a ton. Freight rates have also gone up, as we all know. All these factors have contributed to the increased cost of the feed the poultryman on Vancouver island must purchase. So I do not think it is reasonable to suggest that the prairie farmer has been in any way unfair. I have lived on the prairies too long not to have the greatest sympathy for those farmers. In any event, the cost of feed has gone up, and that is a reality we must face today. I believe now it costs as much on the Pacific coast to purchase feed grain as it costs to buy No. 1 milling grain landed in the United Kingdom.
Then came the greatest catastrophe of all. After all the encouragement given the industry to expand, the government failed to obtain the same type of contract they had previously negotiated with the United Kingdom; in other words the United Kingdom began to curtail its purchases of poultry and poultry products. In the years 1946 and 1947 thousands of tons of poultry products were purchased by the United Kingdom. Now those purchases are being discontinued. Only a few weeks ago the Canadian poultry council stated that the United Kingdom had taken the entire surplus of poultry production ever since 1941; then they added these words: "Now our contracts are obscured by monetary difficulties." They urge the government to seek new markets other than those of the United Kingdom, in order to take care of what they describe as the $40 million worth of eggs now being produced.

According to government statistics her total imports have shown an increase of 38 per cent in the first six months of 1948 as compared with the first six months of 1947. subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext:
May I send it over to you? I find I have not the date on the article.
I should like to continue from the point I left off when interrupted by the minister. If the poultrymen of British Columbia are to be able to cover the overhead on their investment in trying to meet these requests of the department for increased production, then it is essential that production be maintained. I should like to put on the record what I think might be described as the average return which might be received from a first-class flock of hens. It will be a conservative estimate. Let us assume that a hen produces about $6.10 worth of eggs during the year. Feed in British Columbia for a hen that would produce eggs to that value would cost approximately $5.10, which would leave a margin of seventy cents to cover expenses and profit.
On motion of Mr. Pearkes the debate was adjourned.

May I say that I asked the Prime Minister if he would let us go on Friday evenings at six o'clock. I
now change that request to ask if we could go tonight at six o'clock. We have made a great deal of progress this week and I wonder whether whoever is leading the house would consider adjourning now until Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was informed this afternoon that there was some objection to adjourning at six o'clock. We would need the unanimous consent of the house to do so, and the government is prepared to accede if there are no objections.
Carried. .

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well then, we will adjourn.
What will be the business on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday we will first take up the resolution under government notices of motion relating to Newfoundland. The second order of business will be Bill No. 12, an act to amend the statute law. When that is completed, we will take up the resolution we were discussing this afternoon, and when that is completed, the emergency resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question of the order of business, was it not understood that when we finally completed everything in relation to Newfoundland we would return to the debate on the address?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps there was some misunderstanding. After consulting my colleagues, I was told that a motion was made for government notices of motion and government orders to precede other business until the 18th of February. It was for that reason I suggested this order.

The minister will remember that, when this was discussed with me, there was a definite assurance that we would return to the address as soon as the Newfoundland matter was disposed of. That was the understanding I gave to my friends and the understanding upon which we agreed to defer the debate on the address.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will be in his seat on Monday. I suggest that Monday be devoted to the business that has been announced and that at that time a decision be made as to the business to follow.

So long as an attempt is made to clear up the matter.
On motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) the house adjourned at six o'clock.

Monday, February 14, 1949
